I have returned to this establishment on two separate occasions, and the contrast between visits could hardly have been more stark. During my first stay, expectations remained modest—one does not, after all, anticipate luxury at such rates—and fortune smiled upon us in the form of an assignment to the north tower, freshly renovated and mercifully free of incident. The second visit, however, unfolded as a catalogue of small indignities and larger failures, beginning with our approach to the city itself.

A chemical spill on the freeway had transformed what should have been a four-hour journey into an eight-hour ordeal, depositing us at the hotel's entrance at two o'clock in the morning, exhausted and desperate for horizontal repose. We joined what proved to be an interminable queue, inching forward with the patience of penitents, only to witness, moments before reaching the desk, a clerk waving another guest ahead of us. This woman, it transpired, was reporting difficulties with our room—the very accommodation I had reserved. The toilet, she explained, had ceased to function properly, and management promptly reassigned her elsewhere.

When our turn finally arrived, the desk clerk informed me with studied indifference that my reserved king-size non-smoking room had vanished from inventory. What remained were a king-size smoking room or a double-queen non-smoking option. The bitter comedy was not lost on me: they had bestowed our room upon the complaining guest. Fatigue, however, erodes one's capacity for protest, and I accepted the double-queen arrangement, suspecting—correctly, as it happened—that we were inheriting the very room the other woman had abandoned.

The space revealed itself immediately as uninhabitable by any reasonable standard. From the bathroom echoed the amplified spectacle of Fremont Street, an hourly assault of cacophonous celebration. No towels awaited us. The bathroom floor gleamed with moisture, decorated with strands of hair. The carpet beyond squelched underfoot, saturated with water of uncertain origin. Given the late hour and the knowledge that every other establishment had reached capacity, we had little choice. My companion mopped up what he could with a bathmat, and we collapsed into sleep.

Hours later, an obscene gurgling noise roused us at intervals. The toilet was producing bubbles, fountaining water across tile and carpet alike—toilet water, spreading its contamination through our temporary shelter. I could not bring myself to use the fixture, fearing some catastrophic eruption mid-use. The hotel's sole redemption lay in their willingness to refund our payment entirely. One does not often encounter such thoroughgoing squalor.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::be76162e-6297-4c2c-be8b-8be691cc: This is precisely the sort of establishment where one consumes pints whilst clad in tracksuit bottoms, on those particular days when the application of cosmetics feels like an insurmountable task. It is decidedly not the variety of venue that calls for white wine spritzers or cosmopolitans. The chief virtue of this establishment lies in its remarkable affordability. As a member of the Scream Pubs family, it offers drinks prices beginning at a mere £1.80, and should hunger strike, £4-5 will guarantee your departure with stomach thoroughly satisfied. Two pool tables occupy the space, though their unfortunate proximity to one another ensures that patrons find themselves both delivering and receiving unintended blows from pool cues to the back every few minutes at minimum. The downstairs section boasts numerous television screens for the consumption of sporting events, though the dreadful music perpetually assaulting one's ears will certainly inspire regret that you did not simply remain at home to watch the match in the comfort of your own sitting room: the jukebox has been programmed with a particular cunning to play exclusively those songs least selected—which is to say, the truly abysmal tracks that no patron would ever willingly pay to hear—thereby compelling people to insert money for the collective good of changing the selection. And there exist numerous other features that may very well discourage your patronage. To begin with, its subterranean location ensures that the atmosphere remains dark, dingy, and generally rather dispiriting. Add to this unfortunate circumstance the fact that this establishment has not witnessed a proper refurbishment in far too many years, and one encounters a combination of gloom and dreariness thoroughly intermixed with shabbiness and grime. But the single most egregious failing of this place resides in the condition of the lavatories. Without wishing to appear excessively demanding, I maintain certain modest expectations: that toilets should possess a) paper and b) functioning locks upon their doors. Yet when one has spent considerable time queuing for one of merely three facilities—of which one will invariably be out of service—one tends simply to accept these deficiencies with whatever grace can be mustered.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::56d83b20-4592-4ff6-b3ab-c3299c65:
I confess to a fury that lingers still. Having attended pre-release screenings at this particular venue on earlier occasions—occasions marked by competence and order—I arrived to discover chaos so profound, so utterly inexcusable, that the memory provokes indignation even now.

My timing, as always, allowed margin enough for the unforeseen. What I encountered, however, exceeded the boundaries of reasonable anticipation. The queue had been relegated outdoors—this beneath a merciless sun that pressed the thermometer to one hundred ten degrees—and it snaked preposterously around the theater's corner, doubled back upon itself, wound past the elevator banks and the ornamental trees, then climbed the broad front steps in a final, desperate ascent. Very well: the unemployed had evidently stationed themselves before the doors since mid-afternoon, staking their claim four full hours before the seven o'clock showing. Disappointing, perhaps, but hardly catastrophic. I reconciled myself to possible exclusion and remained, observing that newcomers continued to arrive and none were turned away.

What I cannot forgive, what transforms inconvenience into outrage, is this: they possessed a specific allotment of tickets, tangible and numbered, ready for distribution. They might have issued them immediately, releasing those of us destined for disappointment to salvage our evenings elsewhere. At minimum, they might have done so after we had endured ninety minutes beneath that punishing sun, once the serpentine crowd had diminished somewhat. The arithmetic presents no challenge whatsoever—fifteen tickets in hand necessitates counting fifteen individuals to receive them.

Instead, we waited. No explanation materialized at any juncture. Three employees presided over the collection of our home-printed confirmations—an absurd superfluity of labor. One distributed theater passes while two women simply stood there, perspiring. By seven o'clock, when the line showed no sign of resolution, we abandoned the endeavor, concluding that some administrative catastrophe had derailed their timeline entirely. My time, it seems, holds no value whatsoever in their accounting.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::6c998ea5-d795-44ca-8a25-22424b17:
How many chances does one grant a restaurant simply because the location captivates, or because local ownership tugs at some civic sentiment? Everyone speaks reverently of the sticky buns—those legendary pastries that once arrived unbidden at every table—but those days have passed. Now one must request them specifically, a small indignity that prompts uncharitable speculation: perhaps El Chorro can no longer afford such complimentary gestures. More troubling than missing buns, however, is the service provided by most of the female staff. I say this as a woman myself, as someone who has worked in restaurants, as someone whose family once owned dining establishments in Arizona. These servers seem unable to think independently, or perhaps they labor under management that denies them any real authority.

My friends had arrived before me—a party of eight ordering bottles of wine and food, assembled for happy hour though confined to its limited offerings. Another friend and I arrived five minutes after happy hour had officially ended; we had been detained by work. My friend, who was hosting this gathering, walked directly to the waitress as she approached our table and explained, "These are the two ladies I mentioned earlier." The waitress responded with immediate efficiency: happy hour was over. I felt the familiar tightening of disappointment. I ordered a drink and an appetizer, then ventured reasonably, "You see, it's only five minutes past the hour. Given that our friends are ordering quite extensively, couldn't you inquire whether our drinks might still qualify?" She could not, she informed me flatly. Perhaps the manager could bypass the system. But she made no move to ask. I could scarcely believe such inflexibility.

This incident followed an earlier experience that had already colored my impression. On another occasion I had arrived early to meet the same friend and waited outside at the bar, ordering a cocktail. Two women sat to my right, another woman to my left. The two on my right ordered the shrimp appetizer, only to be informed that shrimp was unavailable because of lunch service—would they please select something else? This occurred during the first hour of happy hour. The woman to my left then ordered the shrimp appetizer from the regular menu, not the happy hour selections. Her shrimp arrived promptly. The other ladies and I noticed this contradiction immediately and inquired about it. The female bartender who had declared them out now explained that shrimp was unavailable for happy hour specifically. We pressed further: how were the shrimp different? She insisted they came from different menus, an explanation that satisfied no logical scrutiny. I summoned my bartender, Tim, who fetched the manager. After hearing what had transpired, the manager apologized to both ladies and provided their original order. But the impression had been made, and it adhered stubbornly to all of us. I reported these experiences through my professional network to over six hundred local real estate agents. What a shame for El Chorro—and curiously, these service failures involved only female staff members. Perhaps the male servers can salvage management's reputation.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::aa7ddd1b-2f96-496d-ba44-14337121:
Our earlier immersion in the Mlife spa universe—that luminous afternoon at Vdara's ESPA—had left us hungry for more. We harbored an ambition, perhaps quixotic, to make pilgrimage to every Mlife establishment at least once. On this particular visit, circumstance favored convenience: we had already settled into our hotel rooms, our luggage unpacked, and the prospect of venturing elsewhere held little appeal. The Grand Spa beckoned from within the same building.

I telephoned that very morning, fingers crossed, hoping against hope that appointments might materialize before our evening dinner reservation. Fortune smiled. The woman who answered possessed that particular warmth that immediately puts one at ease, and she managed to slot us in as the final massage appointment of the day. Then came our small disaster: we arrived ten minutes past our designated hour. Any devotee of massage etiquette understands the iron law: tardiness steals from one's own allotted time, not the establishment's schedule.

After the brisk formalities of check-in and payment, we were ushered toward separate changing facilities, each of us assigned a locker. We shed our street clothes with haste, acutely aware of the minutes already lost. Our massage therapists materialized shortly thereafter and guided us through hushed corridors to the treatment room where our couple's massage would unfold. The space itself proved enchanting—warmth radiated from unseen sources, and the atmosphere wrapped around us like cashmere. Both therapists demonstrated exceptional skill; their names have unfortunately dissolved from memory, but their technique remains vivid, hands moving with practiced intelligence across knotted muscles. The session lasted somewhat less than fifty minutes, though we could hardly protest, given our belated arrival.

When the massage concluded, our therapists discreetly withdrew, allowing us privacy for dressing. Upon emerging, we discovered cold water waiting, beaded glasses catching the soft light. My boyfriend and I then separated, each eager to explore the spa facilities during whatever time remained. Though we had been the day's final appointment and closing hour approached, the staff members tending the space never once betrayed impatience or urged us toward the exit. As I wandered through steam rooms and rest areas, conducting my informal inventory of offerings, I found myself quietly disappointed. Given the price—massage plus facility access—I had anticipated something more, particularly regarding the amenities provided for post-treatment preparation. Vdara's spa still held the advantage in that particular dimension. Would I return regardless? Absolutely. What reasonable person refuses pampering when opportunity presents itself?
style_literary_T1.3.coling::8d68dd4d-1de2-4490-8a68-ccd52f7f:
The attractively low rates one encounters in advertisements almost invariably apply to term life insurance—a variety of coverage that carries within it an expiration date, much like milk on a grocery shelf. Term policies serve a targeted, pragmatic function: they provide protection during those years when financial obligations press most heavily upon a household. A parent, for instance, might purchase a twenty-year term that concludes precisely when the youngest child completes university or when the final mortgage payment clears the bank, thereby ensuring that an untimely death will not derail a son's education or compel a grieving widow to abandon the family home. Should the policyholder survive to that appointed hour, however, the contract simply expires, its promise unfulfilled, its premiums vanished into the actuarial ether. Consider the mathematics: the typical purchaser enters the contract in his thirties and maintains coverage through his fifties or perhaps his early sixties—a span during which the overwhelming majority will continue drawing breath. Only a small fraction perish; their claims are financed, in essence, by the premiums collected from the fortunate many who survive.

The arithmetic of profitability becomes transparent when examined closely. Imagine one hundred individuals, each purchasing a policy worth one hundred dollars for an annual premium of ten dollars. Should a single policyholder die, the insurer collects one thousand dollars in premiums, disburses one hundred to the deceased's estate, and retains nine hundred. This surplus does not languish idle; it flows into investments, generating returns that compound the company's advantage. Scale these figures upward—multiply the policyholders into thousands, reduce the mortality rate to fractions of a percentage point—and the potential for profit swells to staggering proportions. Insurance companies further protect their margins through rigorous underwriting, excluding those whose circumstances suggest elevated risk. The terminally ill find coverage elusive or impossible; drivers with checkered records face escalating premiums or outright denial.

In the final analysis, insurance resembles nothing so much as a casino operating in reverse. The industry constructs its edifice upon probability, odds, term length, and countless other variables, always ensuring that the house maintains its edge. One may occasionally strike fortune, as with a quarter transformed into jackpot winnings, but the system endures because most do not.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::1c1fb589-36fc-45ac-bccc-1e9cced6:
Picture Buffalo Wild Wings stripped of its wings. Add, yes, a marginally broader beer selection — though only marginally. On a Thursday afternoon at four o'clock, three companions and I discovered an empty table in this establishment, a find somehow shocking given that the space appeared to accommodate fewer patrons than The Grind manages on its most cramped evenings. We settled in. Ten minutes elapsed before one of my friends, exasperated, rose from her chair and approached a waitress to request menus. Finding staff proved effortless — perhaps twenty-five employees circulated through the room — which made their collective failure to acknowledge our presence all the more peculiar. The waitress handed over a sheet listing their taps and, curiously, a directory of local restaurants willing to deliver to the premises. The fabled bottle list, supposedly their crown jewel, never materialized. As for that delivery arrangement: no thanks, truly.

The tap selection disappointed immediately. An abundance of overpriced local offerings lined up beside mediocre imports — Colorado and Oregon produce exceptional beers, certainly, but featuring Dead Guy Ale hardly constitutes adventurous curation. Not a single sour among them. Our thirst intensified. We established a deadline: fifteen minutes. Should no server solicit our order within that window, we would abandon ship.

A server did eventually materialize, though she directed her attention exclusively toward the other party occupying the remainder of the room. I leaned toward my companions and predicted her next movements: she would avoid our eyes entirely, settle the other table's bill with meticulous care, then vanish without acknowledging our existence. The prophecy fulfilled itself precisely. Throughout her time in our presence, she kept her spine turned toward us, as though we inhabited some invisible realm.

Departing, I intercepted another server to inquire whether our room actually offered table service or whether customers were expected to trek to the bar for their drinks. She confirmed, without meeting my gaze, that yes, the room received service, then pivoted away to study her notepad with sudden fascination.

This operation runs multiple locations. A company commanding such an empire should launch new outposts staffed by servers competent enough to transport one single product from point A to point B. The rudeness may not be universal — I cannot say with certainty — but the three employees I encountered here have ensured I will never engage with a fourth. The tap list lacks imagination. For superior selections, visit Taste of Tops or Brat House, or seek out an intimate establishment like TMI. They serve no food whatsoever. Offering delivery menus does not constitute a kitchen. This remains big business masquerading as something else. The owners cultivate an image of edgy, tattooed, hip authenticity — a local haven for the cool kids. It is not that. It is performance, cynical and hollow.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976:
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey has at last swept across a dominion vast enough that galaxies dwelling in the sparse hinterlands of the cosmos—those territories we call voids—can be identified and measured. Through methods developed by Rojas and collaborators, more than a thousand void galaxies have been extracted from this survey, each inhabiting regions where the density contrast delta rho/rho falls below negative 0.6 on scales exceeding seven inverse Megaparsecs. In the present investigation, we examine the luminosity function of these isolated stellar cities and set their properties against those of galaxies crowding together at higher densities.

Our measurements of the void galaxy luminosity function span the magnitude range from negative 21.5 to negative 14.5 in the r-band photometry of the SDSS. The distribution fits well to a Schechter function, yielding characteristic parameters: a normalization Phi* of 0.19 plus or minus 0.04, multiplied by one-hundredth h cubed per cubic Megaparsec; a characteristic magnitude M_r* minus five log h of negative 19.74 plus or minus 0.11; and a faint-end slope alpha of negative 1.18 plus or minus 0.13. By contrast, galaxies inhabiting the denser walls surrounding voids exhibit a Schechter function with Phi* of 1.42 plus or minus 0.03, M_r* minus five log h of negative 20.62 plus or minus 0.08, and alpha of negative 1.19 plus or minus 0.07.

The fainter characteristic magnitude in voids accords with earlier findings by Rojas and colleagues, confirming that void galaxies shine less brilliantly than their counterparts in denser territories, yet the faint-end slope remains strikingly similar. Further analysis reveals that only wall galaxies in the most crowded environments display a shallower faint-end slope. When we compare void galaxies to wall galaxies sharing similar properties—the bluest specimens, those with Sersic index below two, those with hydrogen-alpha equivalent widths exceeding five Angstroms—the luminosity functions prove remarkably alike in shape, differing only in slightly brighter characteristic magnitudes. This measured alpha near negative 1.2 stands shallower than predictions from cold dark matter models, suggesting that voids harbor fewer dwarf galaxies than theory anticipates.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::a31907c5-c035-4dca-ba29-cb4c6fe3:
What began as a thirst for frozen cocktails culminated, on a Friday night in Queens, in a spectacle of violence that would seem more fitting to a frontier saloon than to the carpeted halls of a modern casino. The occasion was the opening of a Fat Tuesdays bar within the Resorts World Casino, an establishment situated near the runways of JFK airport, where hundreds had gathered in anticipation of iced daiquiris and revelry. Instead, they found themselves witnesses to—or participants in—a melee that would send five people to hospital and result in arrests before the night concluded.

The spark, according to a casino employee who observed the evening's deterioration, was an altercation between two women, both standing in what had become an interminable queue for alcohol. Words were exchanged; positions hardened. What might have remained a minor dispute expanded outward like ripples on water, drawing in friends and bystanders until the conflict had metastasized into something larger and more dangerous than its origins would suggest.

By ten-thirty that evening, the situation had escalated beyond verbal sparring. Patrons seized whatever implements came to hand—chairs, poles, the furniture of leisure repurposed as instruments of assault—and set upon one another with a fury that bewildered those who had come merely to drink. Security personnel converged on the scene, attempting to restore order, but the chaos had achieved its own momentum. Elize Brown, who witnessed the unfolding disorder, described it to CBS2 as an experience of pure uncertainty: "Chairs flying everywhere," she recalled, her words conveying not merely the physical danger but the psychological terror of not knowing what violence might come next.

Cell phone footage captured the worst of it—running crowds, profanities echoing through corridors designed for games of chance rather than combat, the ordinary architecture of entertainment transformed into a battlefield. The aftermath yielded three arrests: Andrew Rivers and Jovan Bovell, both twenty-three, faced charges of disorderly conduct, while Bovell received an additional charge for resisting arrest. Marcus Stewart, thirty years old, was issued two summonses. Four security guards and one police officer sustained injuries serious enough to require medical attention.

Ambulances assembled outside the casino as the night wore on. The damage, when tallied, exceeded four thousand dollars. A Resorts World spokesman, in a statement that mixed contrition with resolve, announced plans to increase security measures and declared that such behavior would find no tolerance at their facility. The promise seemed both necessary and insufficient, a response to chaos that had already occurred.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::f05692cf-092b-40e0-9f4a-d3f7ccd6:
I anticipate disapprobation for what follows, yet I proceed regardless. Famished, I venture forth into the vicious sauna that constitutes Scottsdale during monsoon season, hunting sustenance on a Sunday afternoon. After encountering several establishments observing their Sabbath closures—each a fresh disappointment—I resolved to lower my standards and visit the perpetually underwhelming Schlotsky's Deli on Scottsdale Road. But lo, salvation had arrived: a gleaming new Capriotti's and Everything Bagel had swept in to rescue the neighborhood from mediocrity. Rejoice, I thought. No, wait—suspend all interruptions, for my tale is not concluded.

I cross the threshold and immediately register that the interior temperature hovers around eighty-five degrees. Delightful. Approaching the register to place my order, I inquire of the very pregnant, perspiring young woman behind the counter how recently they had assumed control of the former Schlotsky's location. She responds with an elaborate eye roll, her gaze dropping earthward, muttering that it has been two months, then demands to know what I wish to order. I state my selection. She requests my name to label the order. I provide it. Another magnificent eye roll follows, accompanied by a shrug that communicates perfect indifference—a gesture suggesting the complete collapse of any pretense at caring. She announces, flatly, that she cannot spell. Because I ordinarily remain unconcerned whether my name receives correct orthography or pronunciation, and because on this particular rare occasion I had articulated it phonetically for her convenience, I let the matter pass. But then, positioned directly before me on the customer-facing register screen, appeared her interpretation: corney. I laughed aloud. She scoffed audibly. What? she demands. I am merely amused, I explain, by your rendering of my name. She smirks, declares it functional, and retreats without further acknowledgment. Rather churlish behavior, I must note.

I proceed to the collection area where finished orders emerge, and observe the young man assembling my sandwich—also perspiring profusely, no exaggeration—repeatedly wiping the moisture from his brow with the back of his wrist. Whatever the case, this is Scottsdale. The third employee present was clearly on his lunch break, a fact made evident when he charged past me at full velocity, hurtling across the dining room while clumsily juggling a plastic cup, skidding approximately three feet to an abrupt halt before an unoccupied table, whereupon he collapsed into his seat. I found myself hoping his beverage selection contained no caffeine.

Listen: I acknowledge their youth, I acknowledge the oppressive heat, I acknowledge that one colleague appears constitutionally spastic, I acknowledge her pregnancy, I can even surmise that she may harbor resentment toward her employment, her circumstances, perhaps herself. None of these conditions, however, absolve the fact that these employees actively sought positions within the food service industry—an industry predicated on serving others food. Service necessitates courtesy. Service equally demands professionalism. Where are the responsible adults to guide these novices and instruct them in proper representation of the establishment? The management should be ashamed. The sandwich, incidentally, proved fantastic. My gratitude to the sweating tall youth.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::c7e45e24-dc16-40b2-9030-8200e20e:
They are not free, however—not truly. Both users, regardless of their geographical positions, must secure an internet connection. Even when both parties draw upon freely offered wireless networks, that wifi exists to entice patronage and commerce; someone, somewhere, absorbs the cost. The illusion of costlessness emerges from the internet's borderless architecture. Traditional voice calls and text messages operate differently: your provider must compensate the foreign provider for the service of delivering your call or message across jurisdictional boundaries. These fees, more often than not, are grotesquely inflated. The bottom line remains unchanged—you pay either way, merely through different mechanisms and under different names.

Telephone systems were constructed long ago, in an era when international communication commanded extraordinary expense—and that history established an enduring precedent. Phone companies generally operated as national monopolies, often fortified by legal protections against competition. They would therefore impose steep fees upon other telecommunications firms attempting to route calls into their territories. They could practice this extraction because no alternatives existed, and because most citizens scarcely troubled themselves over international calling costs. In effect, these fees constituted the cream the telecom was permitted to skim as compensation for maintaining an affordable domestic calling infrastructure accessible to ordinary people.

Then the internet arrived, transforming everything. Many internet service providers began as scrappy, competitive startups offering service over existing phone lines—the dial-up era. This meant they remained eager to interconnect freely with content providers, as doing so enhanced their competitiveness by delivering superior service to their customers. Even when separated by vast distances, they could secure inexpensive links through access to "telecom hotels," facilities teeming with companies competing to offer connections between cities, towns, and rural areas alike. Consequently, internet access has become remarkably cheap, while traditional phone providers have failed to keep pace with this transformation.

This history should also illuminate the ongoing debates surrounding net neutrality. As the United States gravitates toward monopolized infrastructure—whereas you could once dial into any dial-up provider, most Americans now face only one or two high-speed cable options—internet service providers are attempting to revert to the old model, where they wielded far greater power over what they charged consumers. In countries maintaining more open infrastructure, such as New Zealand, where you can select any fiber provider within your local exchange from among dozens of options, this proves far less troublesome an issue.

Your existing phone company views you as a customer from whom to extract additional revenue. Skype, by contrast, still hopes simply to make you a customer at all.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::46555368-c6ff-46dc-88fc-bf38c422:
When one observes the relentless drumbeat of criticism on digital forums—those echo chambers where rworldnews and rpolitics hold court—one might easily arrive at the conclusion that the United States has descended into some third-world police state, a place of unremitting dysfunction and despair. The reality, less theatrical but more nuanced, tells a different story altogether: America remains a fundamentally decent place to live, neither the dystopian nightmare of online hyperbole nor the gleaming exception to human folly. Canada, for its part, occupies much the same middle ground—neither vastly superior to its southern neighbor nor appreciably worse, but simply another developed nation navigating the ordinary complexities of modern governance.

Consider what mass migration actually requires. To uproot one's entire existence, to abandon the familiar streets and faces that constitute the only world one has ever known, to begin again in a foreign land with strange customs and uncertain prospects—this demands desperation of a particular intensity. Those contemplating such a leap must believe, with unwavering conviction, that their present circumstances have become truly hopeless. Most Americans, whatever their complaints about healthcare costs or political gridlock, cannot summon this conviction. Their lives, while imperfect, do not justify the extraordinary effort required. Moreover, Canada does not simply throw open its borders to the discontented; a lengthy, expensive, and bureaucratic immigration process awaits those who wish to relocate northward, filtering out all but the most determined or qualified.

Then there are the practical considerations, mundane but decisive. Canada's cost of living exceeds that of most American regions. Its climate, particularly in those areas affordable to newcomers, proves punishingly cold for much of the year. The Canadian dollar hovers around seventy-six cents against its American counterpart, complicating financial calculations. Should a sudden influx of immigrants materialize, the labor market would quickly saturate, rendering moot whatever superior employment protections Canadian law might offer to those unable to secure work in the first place. Both nations, after all, are vast territories with comfortable populations raising families in relative peace, allied rather than antagonistic, governed by systems more similar than different despite the breathless rhetoric suggesting otherwise.

The notion that America teeters on the brink of collapse—this fantasy sustained by idle teenagers who mistake their inability to purchase the latest iPhone for genuine hardship, and by European provocateurs enjoying cheap sport—collapses under scrutiny. Life in the United States, like life in Canada or throughout Europe, contains its share of difficulties and disappointments, its systemic failures and personal frustrations. But for most people, most of the time, existence proves tolerable enough.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::b1217276-7bc0-4410-b466-8118c703:
The road has become a place of torment for Palermo. Roberto Vitiello, the Sicilian club's defender, speaks with quiet determination about reversing fortunes that have grown increasingly dire with each passing week. Since that distant afternoon of November 2—when his side emerged victorious from the San Siro, defeating AC Milan by two goals to nil—the Islanders have found no success whatsoever in their travels. Now, as Sunday's fixture at Udinese approaches, Vitiello sees an opportunity, perhaps a necessity, to arrest this prolonged misery.

Three consecutive defeats have left Palermo wounded and anxious. The most recent setback, a 2-1 loss at home to Milan just last weekend, dropped them to eleventh in the table, a position that speaks neither of safety nor of ambition. Vitiello, contemplating the predicament from his defensive vantage point, understands what must be done.

"We need to keep working hard in order to defend our Serie A status as soon as possible," he told the Italian press, his words carrying the weight of collective disappointment. "We are disappointed not to have collected anything from our last three league games. But we must bounce back. Sunday's game at Udinese is important and we will give our all to clinch our second win on the road this season in Friuli."

Giuseppe Iachini's charges have harvested merely two points from their last six league encounters—a famine that threatens to undermine the season's broader aspirations. Their opponents, Udinese, languish just below them in thirteenth place, separated by a single point, a margin that renders Sunday's contest particularly consequential.

The Friuli side present their own vulnerabilities. Having fallen to bottom-dwelling Parma in midweek, they appear fragile within their own stadium, winless now in four matches. Coach Andrea Stramaccioni seeks answers, demanding from his players a response worthy of their capabilities.

"Against Parma, we had the wrong approach to the game," he acknowledged. "My players underestimated Parma and we paid the price. We lacked determination and didn't take a shot on goal. Now we must turn the page immediately and show against Palermo the real Udinese."

At Friuli, Udinese have managed only one victory in their last nine home fixtures—a statistic that might embolden visiting sides, were Palermo's own away form not so catastrophically poor. Both teams will field depleted squads: the hosts missing defender Ivan Piris and midfielder Giampiero Pinzi to suspension, while Palermo travel without midfielder Edgar Barreto, sidelined three weeks with muscular damage.

Yet Palermo possess a weapon of considerable potency in Paulo Dybala. The Argentine forward, with thirteen goals already this season, will spearhead the Rossaneri attack, Franco Vazquez operating in support. Upon his shoulders rests much of Sunday's hope.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::1d5a005f-1162-4f21-a546-b8229951:
Here exists, one might say, a textbook instance of that ancient hypocrisy: "do as I say, not as I do." The United States—whether for laudable reasons or lamentable ones—has cast itself in the role of global constabulary, thereby arrogating to itself the authority to prescribe what actions other nations may or may not undertake. Most observers concede that tyrannical despots suffering from mental instability ought not to possess nuclear arsenals; consequently, the international community tends to acquiesce, however grudgingly, to American intervention in such matters.

Yet we must be precise: there exists no genuine "acquiescence" in any meaningful sense. These interventions simply occur. Other nations refrain from protest not from approval but from pragmatism—complaint would achieve nothing of substance. Even were they so inclined, they could impose no sanctions of consequence upon the United States. To address the broader question more directly: America retains its nuclear prerogative because it pioneered these weapons first. No authority existed to prevent their initial development. Once the United States had amassed a substantial stockpile, the permanence of its nuclear status became self-evident; disputing this reality would prove futile. Indeed, one might reasonably argue that American nuclear supremacy has paradoxically reduced proliferation elsewhere. The protective umbrella that the United States extends over its numerous allies means these nations need not pursue their own weapons programs. Thus, counterintuitively, American hegemony has resulted in fewer warheads rather than more.

Virtually every nation acknowledges the necessity of constraining the development and production of nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons. The United States does not stand alone in this conviction. Through the United Nations non-proliferation treaty and various classified accords nested within it, the United States receives authorization to provide nuclear weapons to select NATO allies. This same treaty, however, condemns nuclear weapons development and testing in all other contexts. Because America operates within treaty bounds, and because it participates in UN peacekeeping operations, the responsibility falls to it to condemn other nations attempting to develop nuclear capabilities and to intervene when circumstances demand.

The reality, though rarely articulated plainly, runs thus: one nation possesses military might exceeding that of all others combined. You oppose this nation's invasion of some distant territory. What course lies open to you? You might stand firm, fight back, and perish. You might voice objection, suffer public humiliation, face ostracism, and slide into obscurity. Or you might hold your tongue and accommodate yourself to circumstances. Thus far, everyone who has survived chose the final option.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::8986a229-067f-4f9d-8d01-514889d3:
Should a syllabus for the Biology class find its way into your hands before the semester begins, read it with care and deliberation—for within those pages lie the regulations that will govern your work, the materials you must procure, and sundry other details essential to your success. Return to this document not once but repeatedly, consulting it before each class meeting to ensure that no requirement has slipped your mind. To fix the syllabus firmly in memory, employ the time-honored methods of annotation: let your highlighter illuminate key passages, let your pen underline crucial phrases, let marginal notes capture your understanding.

The techniques of active reading are manifold and complementary. Underlining draws the eye to essential points; highlighting bathes important information in color; a star sketched in the margin flags what demands particular attention; a box drawn around sentences or entire paragraphs creates visual boundaries that aid recall; notes inscribed either on separate paper or on the syllabus's verso transform passive reading into active engagement. Such practices, faithfully observed, serve as bulwarks against forgetfulness.

Before you mark the syllabus itself, however, secure your teacher's permission—some instructors prefer their documents to remain pristine. Should you wish to annotate freely, make a copy using a scanner, thereby creating multiple versions. Keep one syllabus unmarked, a clean reserve; mark the other as thoroughly as you please. Thus, when revisions arrive or circumstances shift, you possess an unblemished original upon which to record new observations.

For students who find themselves without access to scanning equipment at home, several alternatives present themselves. The nearest public library almost certainly maintains a scanner available for patron use; bring your syllabus there, and for a modest fee—rarely exceeding twenty cents per page—reproduce it. Another solution exists for those who carry smartphones or tablets equipped with cameras. Install one of the many applications designed specifically for document scanning; these ingenious programs allow you to photograph a page and transform that image into PDF, DOC, or various other digital formats. If neither option proves practicable, do not suffer in silence. Ask whether the school itself maintains scanning facilities, or whether your Biology teacher might scan the syllabus on your behalf. They will almost certainly oblige.

Most science classes, Biology among them, require students to pay a laboratory fee. This charge, typically collected during the first week of instruction, funds the materials necessary for experimental work—the chemicals, slides, specimens, and equipment that make scientific inquiry possible. In most instances the fee is refundable: when the course concludes, the money returns to you. Should you damage laboratory property through carelessness, however, expect no refund. Handle all materials with respect, whether they pose danger or seem innocuous.

Nearly every class demands that students bring pencils or pens and paper for note-taking. Even when your teacher does not explicitly require these implements, bring them regardless and use them diligently. The act of writing reinforces learning, allowing you to retain information more securely and providing material for later review. Master effective note-taking techniques to amplify your success; consult the second part of this guide for detailed instruction.

Arrive at class with your materials already arranged before you—pencils sharpened, notebook open, the previous day's homework visible. This preparation hastens your readiness and spares you the indignity of rummaging through your bag while instruction proceeds. Set out your supplies immediately upon sitting down, unless your teacher specifically requests that you keep everything stowed until given permission. These moments before class formally begins also offer an excellent opportunity to review yesterday's assignments and notes, confirming that nothing has gone missing and refreshing your memory of what came before.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::ab8e7c37-fe1e-4b22-8440-e3a25a67:
Having concluded the discussion that follows, I turned to the authors' earlier work—the MUS-ROVER system upon which this present paper rests its foundations. The exercise proved illuminating in two respects: first, it deepened my comprehension of the current submission considerably; second, and more troubling, it revealed itself as indispensable to that comprehension, a necessity that speaks to deficiencies in the paper itself.

My overall assessment remains conflicted. Though I find myself drawn to this work—and though the terrain it covers holds no mysteries for me, familiar as I am with the Bach chorales, with probabilistic reasoning, with n-gram models and their cognates—I discovered the exposition frustratingly opaque in numerous passages. The proliferation of mathematical notation, rather than clarifying the argument, too often obscured it beneath a thicket of symbols.

The underlying ideas possess genuine merit, the approaches demonstrate real ingenuity, and both warrant publication and further exploration. Yet I harbor reservations about whether ICLR, in its present configuration, offers the appropriate forum for this paper as it now stands. My concern stems neither from the musical application—such domains can prove remarkably fertile ground for computational inquiry—nor necessarily from the methodological choices themselves. Rather, what troubles me is the mismatch between ambition and available space. A journal article, with its more generous page allowances, would grant the authors room to unfold these concepts deliberately: to furnish illuminating examples traced through their complete development, to establish the requisite background both for their previous system and for the broader intellectual context, to demonstrate the approach's generality through application to additional datasets beyond the single corpus here examined. The conference format compresses everything into such density that the work, however strong its foundations, becomes nearly impenetrable. Isolating one component for focused treatment might resolve this constraint, though I cannot envision precisely what form such extraction should take.

Were the authors to undertake substantial revision—though I confess myself unable to prescribe the specific path within the prevailing length limitations—I would reconsider my evaluation favorably. The greater investment, however, would yield richer returns as an expansive, pellucid journal contribution.

[Addendum: subsequent discussions and authorial revisions have prompted me to adjust my assessment accordingly]
style_literary_T1.3.coling::ce094fc2-a215-4a99-a6f1-dc2a198d:
Energy is not, strictly speaking, a substance that migrates bodily through space like water flowing through pipes. Rather, it exists as an intrinsic property of objects themselves—a quality that inheres in matter and can be transmuted from one form into another through the performance of work. Consider the example of pushing a ball uphill: the chemical energy residing in your muscles undergoes conversion, first into the kinetic energy of the ball's motion, then into potential energy as the sphere ascends against gravity's insistent pull. You "bestow" energy upon the ball not through any mystical transfer, but through the pedestrian mechanism of work—which is to say, by exerting force across distance, that most fundamental of physical operations.

Yet to probe deeper into this mechanism, we must acknowledge that energy's transmission depends intimately upon the character of materials themselves. In gases, energy lodges within the trembling vibrations between molecular bonds, then cascades onward as momentum into neighboring particles—what we call thermal energy. Metals conduct this restless energy through their crystalline lattices in waves of atomic oscillation. Certain exotic materials, perovskites among them, respond to mechanical strain by releasing electrical charges when their internal atomic arrangements shift. Throughout all these transformations runs a single governing principle: energy represents the inexorable passage from enthalpy—which is order, structure, arrangement—toward entropy's welcoming chaos, driven by nothing more than probability's patient arithmetic that disorder must increase across time's arrow.

When you move a ball, you impose your conscious will upon its stable repose. Chemical reactions in your arm's musculature demand that protein fibers contract, propelling your rigid skeletal levers forward. At the point of contact between your solid hand and the ball's surface, strong nuclear forces between atoms accomplish the actual exchange: atomic nuclei in your palm repel those in the ball's surface, and this repulsion constitutes the transfer. Because the forces binding ball to table and ball to air prove weaker than the chemical energy marshaled in your arm, the ball yields and rolls forward. Chemical energy itself derives from electrons seeking their most stable orbital configurations, those arrangements again dictated by fundamental atomic forces.

Or, to speak plainly: energy is simply the property of having abundance. Whatever possesses abundance cannot help but share when it encounters scarcity. Run a mile, and you must spend a portion of your metabolic reserves on muscles, on friction with the ground, on air resistance. Persuade a friend to wash dishes, and you expend a different currency entirely—social capital, perhaps, or actual cookies—to accomplish work by proxy.
style_literary_T1.3.coling::da2d8730-7c13-4b32-befb-c2bbe666:
Section 51(xxxi) stands as a particular subclause within the broader architecture of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia, occupying a modest yet crucial place in the framework of federal power.

This provision empowers the Commonwealth Parliament to enact legislation concerning the acquisition of property from private holders, but it does so with an essential qualification: any such acquisitions undertaken by the federal government must be conducted on just terms, a requirement that injects both principle and practical constraint into what might otherwise become an unchecked exercise of sovereign authority.

The provision is sometimes referred to, in the compressed shorthand of legal practitioners and constitutional scholars alike, as the 'just terms' provision—a phrase that captures its essence while eliding its complexity.

Beyond its considerable importance to the domains of Australian Constitutional Law and Property Law, the section has achieved a peculiar distinction for its role as a plot device in The Castle, that iconic Australian film which transformed a technical constitutional question into populist narrative, making household words of concepts that might otherwise have languished in law libraries and seminar rooms.

Text
Section 51(xxxi) reads, in the spare and measured language characteristic of constitutional drafting, as follows:

Jurisprudence
While section 51(xxxi) was consciously adapted from the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution, drawing upon that earlier experiment in limiting governmental power over private property, the Australian provision exhibits many significant differences from its American antecedent, differences that have shaped its operation and constrained its reach.

The 'just terms' requirement, despite its placement within federal constitutional text, has been held by the courts not to affect or bind the State Parliaments in their own exercises of compulsory acquisition power, a limitation that reflects the federal structure of Australian governance.

In the landmark case of Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth, decided in 1946, Justice Dixon offered an illuminating statement regarding the purpose underlying this constitutional safeguard, observing that the inclusion of the 'just terms' condition was intended "to prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject"—a formulation that grounds the provision in principles of fairness and restraint.

The interpretation that the High Court of Australia has given to the critical terms "acquisition" and "just terms" has had the practical effect, however, of limiting the protection that section 51(xxxi) affords to property rights, rendering it a more modest shield than might initially appear. Moreover, the provision operates only at those particular times when the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property, not as a general prohibition on interference. As such, it functions as a contingent guarantee, activated by specific governmental action, rather than constituting a general constitutional right or fundamental freedom to enjoy property rights without disturbance.

The Commonwealth may acquire property on just terms only for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws"—a requirement that ties the acquisition power to the enumerated heads of Commonwealth legislative competence. This constitutional architecture means that every law supported by section 51(xxxi) must derive its constitutional validity from that provision itself, and not be supported by any other additional legislative power that might allow circumvention of the 'just terms' requirement.

Property
The High Court of Australia has consistently taken a wide and generous view of the fundamental concept of "property" as it appears in the constitutional text. Several members of the court seized the opportunity to consider the meaning and scope of the term property in the case of Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel, decided in 1944, establishing principles that would guide subsequent interpretation. Justice Starke articulated a capacious definition, declaring that the term includes "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action"—a catalogue that spans from the tangible to the abstract. Justice McTiernan, reinforcing this expansive approach, confirmed that the term property extends comprehensively to both tangible and intangible forms of holding.

An instructive example of the breadth of the concept of property within the operation of section 51(xxxi) is provided by the celebrated case of Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth, commonly known as the Bank Nationalisation Case, which tested the limits of governmental power in the charged atmosphere of post-war reconstruction. In that consequential litigation, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banking institutions through a complex mechanism involving the vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth, followed by the subsequent appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon, examining these provisions with characteristic analytical precision, characterised them as removing effective control over the property of the private banks, stripping the nominal owners of meaningful authority. He concluded that this displacement of control constituted, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right, even absent formal transfer of title.

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests in certain contexts, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property falling within section 51(xxxi), because licence conditions are inherently susceptible to modification and change by the very governmental authority that granted them.

Acquisition
For the purposes of applying section 51(xxxi), property must actually have been acquired by somebody—a positive transfer must occur—and the acquisition must be undertaken for a Commonwealth purpose, not merely as an incidental effect of regulation. This requirement stands in sharp contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution, where the destination of the property does not ultimately matter; under American constitutional law it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in the recent case of JT International SA v Commonwealth, the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which significantly restricted the plaintiff's commercial use of its valuable trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth actually acquiring any property for itself. Similarly, in Cunningham v Commonwealth, the High Court determined that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass privileges for retired members of Parliament did not constitute an acquisition of property within the meaning of the constitutional provision.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth, the High Court held that a financial grant to New South Wales which was expressly tied to that State compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just, the Commonwealth being unable to accomplish indirectly what it could not do directly. The validity of a grant made in the absence of any requirement to acquire property was subsequently upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw, clarifying the boundaries of permissible federal-state arrangements.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms based upon the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the constitutional requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement embedded in the American Fifth Amendment, however, the phrase "just terms" imports no strict equivalence to market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair," or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair" in all the circumstances. However, this judgment of "fairness" must take comprehensive account of all the interests affected by the acquisition, not merely those of the dispossessed owner whose property has been taken.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily demand that a complete compensation package be presented as an integral part of the acquisition scheme itself. It is constitutionally sufficient that the legislative scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation after the fact. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures with considerable care to ensure their adequacy and fairness.

There may exist some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) simply does not apply, such as those acquisitions made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution, which grants plenary power over the territories.

Section 51(xxxi) represents an exception to the usual norm governing interpretation of the various subsections of section 51—namely, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" or narrow another. In this particular case, however, the Court has determined that it will not allow another grant of legislative power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation carefully imposed upon the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act of 1906, largely drafted by the capable hand of Littleton Groom, was the first Commonwealth statute to address systematically the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government. Its most contentious provision proved to be a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining activities on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for administering compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act of 1945 compulsorily acquired substantial areas of land owned by Chinese-Australian residents in Darwin, leading directly to the end of the local Chinatown community that had existed there. The discriminatory legislation was first suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott, who explicitly proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of freehold land to leasehold tenure in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past," revealing the racial animus underlying the proposal. Abbott stated plainly that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again," making no effort to disguise his intentions. He further observed, with cold bureaucratic calculation, that "if land is acquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets." The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during wartime bombing, and the former Chinatown residents returned after the war's conclusion only to find their homes and businesses reduced to rubble and ashes.

The camera's unsteady eye has captured what now requires explanation: a police officer beating and Tasering a seventeen-year-old boy during what began as an ordinary traffic stop in Virginia. The footage, which an officer allegedly attempted to expunge from existence but did not, has compelled an investigation into conduct that defies easy justification.

Brandon Wyne occupied the backseat of his friend Courtney Griffith's vehicle on the tenth of January when they were stopped for nothing more consequential than a broken tail light. Griffith, eighteen years old, was driving. What followed transformed a minor mechanical infraction into something far more troubling.

As the officers approached the stopped car, they announced they detected the odor of marijuana and commanded all occupants to exit immediately. Griffith maintained that she permits no marijuana in her vehicle and insisted upon being presented with a warrant for arrest. Wyne stated his willingness to comply with one stipulation: that no officer lay hands upon him until his mother could arrive, as he remained legally a minor. His assertion of this right ignited an argument.

Griffith's cell phone captured what came next. The footage shows the officer retaliating against the boy's request by directing pepper spray into his eyes. Wyne can be seen clutching his face, screaming in agony, crying out his age as if it were a shield: "I'm seventeen years old! Stop!" He raises both hands skyward, palms open, shouting "Stop! Stop!" The officer's response arrives in measured words—"you're going to get it again"—followed by action: the Taser's electrodes deliver their voltage not once but twice.

The recording ceases only when both Wyne and Griffith have been forcibly removed from the vehicle and an officer notices the phone propped against the dashboard. Seizing it, he halts the documentation. The footage surfaced months afterward when Griffith discovered it residing in her phone's "Recently Deleted" folder, where someone had attempted to consign it to digital oblivion.

Virginia Beach Police Chief Jim Cervera, confronted with the images, offered words weighted with visible discomfort to the local television station: "There's some things I saw in that that I do not feel comfortable with." He indicated his department would examine whether evidence tampering had occurred. The official statement that followed announced the placement of the officer in question on administrative duty while the investigation proceeds—a bureaucratic formulation that suspends judgment while acknowledging that judgment must inevitably arrive. The video endures despite efforts to erase it, and what it depicts cannot be unseen or easily reconciled with the ordinary expectations of lawful authority.

Two bank robbers operating across the Pittsburgh region are believed to possess military or law enforcement training, prompting the FBI to classify them as armed and exceptionally dangerous. Throughout the early months of this year, a pair of masked gunmen wielding handguns have struck three separate financial institutions, executing their most recent assault on the tenth of April. Surveillance cameras have captured these unknown assailants in the act of pressing loaded weapons directly against the temples of terrified bank employees, uttering threats that escalate beyond mere theft—they have vowed to abduct hostages and open fire upon any police officers who dare engage them in confrontation.

Yet it is the manner in which these two criminals manipulate their firearms that has drawn the sharpest attention from federal investigators. The way they grip, aim, and carry their weapons suggests a discipline acquired through formal instruction, leading authorities to entertain a disturbing possibility: these thieves may themselves be former officers of the law, individuals who once stood on the opposite side of justice.

Video footage reveals one masked robber maintaining his index finger extended along the barrel of his pistol, positioned deliberately away from the trigger mechanism—a safety protocol drilled into law enforcement personnel during their most elementary training. Both suspects, clad in dark sweatpants and matching sweatshirts, display athletic prowess as they vault over counters with practiced ease at the commencement of each heist. Patrick Fallon, speaking on behalf of the FBI, emphasized the significance of these observations: "These folks have some kind of training in firearms, meaning they could be former military, they could be law enforcement, either former or current." He noted further that common street criminals rarely employ holsters, another telling detail captured on camera.

Both men stand between five feet eight inches and five feet nine inches tall, possessing what witnesses describe as excellent physical conditioning. During each robbery, one assailant positions himself behind the counter to gather currency while his confederate maintains control through intimidation, keeping bank personnel frozen under the threat of his weapon.

Authorities have observed an unsettling pattern: the criminals grow increasingly aggressive and violent with each successive strike, their raids on January twenty-fourth, February twenty-first, and April tenth demonstrating an alarming escalation. The suspects are described as white males of medium to larger build, their muscular frames suggesting dedicated physical training. They have been observed fleeing in an unremarkable gray Toyota Corolla, one of the world's most ubiquitous automobiles—a deliberate choice designed to ensure anonymity. Both men apparently hail from Pittsburgh itself, their regional accents betraying local origins. Investigators suspect the baggy clothing is discarded immediately following each escape. The FBI has posted a reward of ten thousand dollars for information culminating in their capture.

Judith Scott, who came into the world on the first of May in 1943 and departed it on the fifteenth of March in 2005, was an American fiber sculptor whose work achieved international renown despite—or perhaps because of—the profound challenges that marked her existence from its very beginning. Born with Down Syndrome and rendered deaf through childhood illness, she would ultimately discover in abstract fiber art a language more eloquent than speech, a means of communication that transcended the limitations imposed upon her by biology and circumstance. Her enrollment in 1987 at Oakland's Creative Growth Art Center, an institution dedicated to supporting individuals with developmental disabilities, proved the catalyst for an artistic awakening of remarkable intensity and originality. The story of her life has been preserved in Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott, a memoir published in 2016 by her twin sister, who witnessed both the cruelties inflicted upon Judith and her ultimate triumph.

Judith entered the world in Cincinnati, Ohio, on that spring day in 1943, arriving alongside her fraternal twin Joyce into a middle-class family that already included older brothers. Unlike her twin, Judith bore the chromosomal signature of Down Syndrome, a difference that would shape every aspect of her existence. During infancy, she contracted Scarlet Fever, and the illness stole her hearing—a loss that would remain undetected for years, compounding the difficulties she already faced. For the first seven and a half years of her life, Judith remained at home with her parents, her twin sister, and her brothers, living within the warm orbit of family. Though the developmental chasm between the two girls widened with each passing month, their parents made conscious, deliberate efforts to treat these youngest children equally, to refuse the easy inequity that circumstance seemed to invite.

But when the time arrived for formal schooling to begin, Judith was deemed "ineducable" by the authorities who controlled such determinations. The single classroom reserved for children with disabilities required passage of verbally-based entrance examinations, and Judith, her deafness still unrecognized, could not navigate these linguistic barriers. Acting upon medical advice—counsel that future generations would surely question—her parents made the agonizing decision to place Judith in the Columbus State Institution, formerly known as the Columbus State School, a facility designed for the mentally disabled. The date was October 18, 1950, and the separation carved a wound in both twins that would never entirely heal.

The institutional records from Judith Scott's early years in that place assigned her an IQ of thirty, a number derived from oral testing administered before anyone understood that she could not hear the questions being posed to her. This assessment, tragically flawed in its methodology, condemned her to a life without training, without education, without opportunity for growth. Torn from her twin, Judith descended into severe alienation, and behavioral difficulties emerged with increasing frequency. Her Clinical Record, written in the cold, bureaucratic language of institutional assessment, documented the deterioration: "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." The institution's response was to transfer her to an even smaller facility in Gallipolis, Ohio, further isolating her from everything familiar.

Thirty-five years passed before Joyce Scott, through lengthy and extraordinarily difficult negotiations, secured legal guardianship of her sister and brought Judith to California in 1985. California, unlike Ohio, recognized the rights of all mentally disabled citizens to continuing education, and this legal framework made possible what love alone could not accomplish. Judith Scott would die of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, just weeks before her sixty-second birthday, having outlived her birth life expectancy by nearly half a century.

On the first of April in 1987, Judith Scott began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the pioneering organizations in the world dedicated to providing studio space for artists with disabilities. For almost two years, she showed little interest in artistic activity of any kind. Her efforts with paint proved unremarkable. She scribbled loops and circles without representational intent, displaying such profound disinterest that the staff seriously contemplated terminating her participation in the program. Then, quite by chance, Judith observed a fiber art class being conducted by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy, and in that moment of casual observation, her artistic breakthrough occurred.

Using whatever materials lay within reach, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically innovative form of artistic expression. While other students practiced conventional stitching techniques, she began sculpting with unprecedented zeal and concentration, displaying creative gifts and absolute focus that the staff immediately recognized as extraordinary. Granted complete freedom to select her own materials, she gathered whatever objects she encountered—regardless of their ownership, a detail that became part of her creative practice—and wrapped them in carefully chosen colored yarns, building diverse sculptures of widely varying shapes and sizes. Some of her creations resembled cocoons or fragments of the human body, while others took the form of elongated totemic poles reaching upward. Many works featured pairs of forms, echoing and honoring her lifelong experience as a twin. For eighteen years, five days each week, Judith labored at her art, ultimately producing more than two hundred pieces.

Her first exhibition arrived in 1999, coinciding with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott, and together these events launched her toward worldwide recognition. Scott's work achieved immense popularity within the world of outsider art, and her pieces now command substantial sums. She is hailed today not merely as an outsider but as a contemporary artist of consequence, her work held in the permanent collections of numerous prestigious institutions: the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan; the American Visionary Art Museum in Baltimore; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; the Museum of American Folk Art in Manhattan; Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art in Chicago; the Irish Museum of Modern Art in Dublin; the Oakland Museum; L'Aracine Musée d'Art Brut in Paris; the Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection in Paris and Prague; and the Collection de l'art brut in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Her exhibition history includes numerous notable shows: a 2018 retrospective at Creative Growth; the 2014-15 Bound and Unbound at the Brooklyn Museum; appearances at the 2017 Venice Biennale; presentations at the National Gallery of Art in Washington and the New Museum of Contemporary Art in New York; and many others across continents and decades, each testament to an artistic vision that emerged from silence and isolation to speak a universal language of form, color, texture, and profound human creativity.

style_literary_T1.7.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation peak—visible in cosmic matter distribution up to redshifts approaching 3.5—testifies to the sustained expansion of that sonic horizon first detected in the temperature anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. Today, observers can locate this peak's position with remarkable fidelity: galaxy surveys achieve precision better than one percent, while measurements drawn from Lyman-alpha forests and quasar clustering reach accuracies of 1.4 to 1.6 percent. When combined with the Alcock-Paczyński effect, which emerges from the evolving ratio between angular and spatial or redshift dimensions of spherically symmetric source distributions across cosmic distances, the BAO measurement stands as one of our most formidable instruments for probing the Universe's underlying geometry. In the present work, we deploy five BAO peak measurements extracted from the final data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's fourth iteration, spanning mean redshifts at 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48, and 2.33, to conduct a direct, rigorous comparison between the standard Lambda-CDM cosmology and one of its principal rivals, the R_h=ct universe. For thoroughness, we supplement the Alcock-Paczyński diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe that presumes a constant comoving distance scale. Both diagnostics remain unburdened by uncertain parameters—the Hubble constant among them—and therefore prove ideally suited to this exercise in model selection. We discover that the R_h=ct framework earns favor from these measurements over the standard model when judged solely through the Alcock-Paczyński effect, commanding a likelihood near 75 percent against roughly 25 percent, whereas Planck-Lambda-CDM gains the advantage over R_h=ct when assessed solely through the volume-averaged distance probe, with a likelihood approaching 80 percent versus 20 percent. A joint analysis employing both probes yields an inconclusive result, granting comparable likelihoods to each cosmology. Consequently, we cannot affirm through this investigation that BAO data, considered independently, vindicate an accelerating Universe.

We introduce here what we have chosen to call the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate'—a new approach to artificial intelligence that draws selected attributes from objects dwelling in disparate domains (chess problems, say, or classical music, or paintings that have earned their place in the canon) and recombines these elements in such fashion as to generate novel attributes capable, in principle, of creating objects that humans might value as genuinely creative work within any of the source domains. By this method, some portion of the burden of generating creative content passes from human hands to mechanical process.

We tested this approach within the particular domain of chess problem composition. Employing it, we automatically composed numerous sets of problems, basing them upon attributes we had extracted and recombined from several sources: chess problems and tournament games played by humans, renowned paintings, abstract art evolved by computational means, photographs capturing human faces and forms, and tracks of classical music. The quality of these generated problems was then assessed by two methods—automatically, using an existing and experimentally validated computational model of chess aesthetics, and also by human experts whose judgment in the domain has been earned through long practice.

The results suggest that attributes collected from chess and from other, seemingly foreign domains, then recombined using our approach, can indeed produce chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. Most striking: a source of low quality within chess itself—that is, tournament game sequences played between weak competitors—when combined with actual photographs of people, proved able to produce three-move problems of quality comparable to, or surpassing, those generated using a high-quality chess source such as published compositions by acknowledged experts. Moreover, it did so with greater efficiency. Why information drawn from a foreign domain should integrate and function in this curious way remains, for now, an open question. The approach is, in principle, both scalable and applicable to any domain in which objects possess attributes representable by real numbers.
