Here we encounter one of those perennial ironies: the injunction to "do as I say, not as I do." The United States, for better or worse, has cast itself in the role of global constabulary, thereby arrogating to itself the authority to prescribe the behavior of sovereign nations. Few would dispute the premise that unstable autocrats—men of volatile temperament and unchecked ambition—ought not to possess nuclear armaments; consequently, the international community tends to acquiesce, more or less tacitly, to American interventions.

But let us be precise: there exists no "acquiescence" in any meaningful sense. Events simply unfold. Other nations refrain from protest not from consent but from pragmatic calculation—their objections would accomplish little. They lack the leverage to impose sanctions of any consequence upon Washington, even were they so inclined. To address the broader question: the United States maintains its nuclear arsenal because it pioneered these weapons before any authority existed to prohibit their development. Once America had accumulated a substantial stockpile, the reality of its nuclear status became immutable, rendering further dispute futile.

Indeed, one might argue that American nuclear capacity has paradoxically limited proliferation. The United States extends its protective umbrella over numerous allies, obviating their need to pursue independent weapons programs. This arrangement, whatever its other implications, has likely resulted in fewer nuclear arsenals worldwide. It bears emphasizing that virtually every nation recognizes the imperative to constrain the development and deployment of nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons. America hardly stands alone in this conviction.

Thanks to the United Nations' nonproliferation treaty—and the classified protocols embedded within it—the United States retains authorization to supply nuclear weapons to select NATO partners. This same treaty, however, proscribes the creation and testing of such weapons under nearly all other circumstances. Because Washington operates within the treaty's provisions, and because the United States constitutes a pillar of UN peacekeeping operations, it assumes responsibility for censuring nations that pursue nuclear weapons programs and for deploying force when circumstances demand. The United Nations has, in effect, deputized America as global enforcer, though member states routinely lament that delegation of authority.

Consider the arithmetic of power: one country commands military resources exceeding those of all others combined. When that country undertakes an invasion you oppose, what recourse remains? You might resist openly, invite destruction, and perish. You might voice dissent, endure public humiliation, face ostracism, and sink into irrelevance. Or you might remain silent and accommodate yourself to circumstances. Thus far, all who have survived have chosen the third path—a testament not to justice but to the cold logic of disproportionate force.
style_literary_T1.7.coling::8986a229-067f-4f9d-8d01-514889d3:
Should a syllabus for the Biology course be available, examine it with care before attending the initial class meeting, absorbing its rules, its catalog of required materials, its calendar of obligations and deadlines. Return to this document habitually—indeed, each morning before class convenes—as a safeguard against oversight and forgetfulness. To impress the syllabus upon memory, employ the familiar arsenal of active reading: highlight passages in translucent color, underline phrases that demand attention, inscribe marginal annotations that translate the instructor's language into your own understanding.

The methods of engaging a syllabus are manifold and complementary. Underlining captures essential statements; highlighting bathes crucial information in chromatic emphasis; a hand-drawn star signals matter of particular importance; a carefully ruled box isolates key sentences or entire paragraphs from their surroundings; notes transcribed onto separate paper, or upon the verso of the syllabus itself, create a parallel text of your own devising. These techniques, applied judiciously, ensure that nothing vital escapes recollection. Before marking the original document, however, secure the instructor's permission—some educators prefer their syllabi remain pristine. Should you wish to preserve both an unmarked original and an annotated copy, employ a scanner to produce duplicates. This practice proves especially valuable should the syllabus undergo revision mid-semester, allowing fresh annotations on the duplicate while the original remains untouched.

Students lacking access to scanning equipment at home possess several alternatives. The nearest public library typically maintains scanning facilities, charging no more than twenty cents per page—a modest investment in academic preparation. Those who carry smartphones or tablets equipped with cameras may install applications designed specifically for document digitization. These programs transform photographed pages into PDF files, Word documents, and various other digital formats. Should neither option prove feasible, approach the school administration or the Biology instructor directly; they invariably welcome such requests and gladly provide assistance.

Most science courses, Biology among them, assess students a laboratory fee. This charge underwrites the materials required for experimental work—the slides and specimens, the chemicals and glassware that make empirical investigation possible. Instructors generally permit at least the first week of the term for payment. In most cases the fee proves refundable: upon successful completion of the course, the money returns to students' hands. Should a student damage equipment, however—whether through carelessness or misfortune—the fee typically remains forfeit. Handle all laboratory materials, hazardous and benign alike, with appropriate caution and respect.

Although not every instructor explicitly requires writing implements and paper for note-taking, their utility transcends formal requirement. Bring them regardless. The act of transcribing information aids retention; notes taken during class sessions become invaluable resources during subsequent review. To maximize the effectiveness of this practice, cultivate strong note-taking skills through deliberate study and application. Consult resources devoted to this essential academic craft for detailed guidance and methodology.

Before each class session begins, prepare your workspace by arranging necessary materials within easy reach—this simple ritual accelerates your readiness and prevents the awkward disruption of rummaging through your bag when the lesson has already commenced. Defer this preparation only if the instructor specifically requests that students leave materials untouched until given explicit permission. These moments before class also offer opportunity to review the previous day's homework and notes, confirming completeness and refreshing memory of recently acquired knowledge.
style_literary_T1.7.coling::33c5609d-3402-4e52-abb9-f74944f2:
In the harsh glare of cell phone footage, a Virginia traffic stop has unraveled into something darker: a police officer beating and Tasering a seventeen-year-old boy, then allegedly attempting to erase the evidence of his own conduct. The video, grainy yet damning, has triggered an investigation — not merely into what transpired that January evening, but into whether an officer of the law tried to make the truth disappear.

Brandon Wyne sat in the backseat of his friend's vehicle, Courtney Griffith behind the wheel, when the blue lights flashed behind them on the tenth of January. The stated violation: a broken tail light, that minor mechanical failure that so often serves as pretext. Griffith, eighteen years old, pulled over. What followed would be captured in fragments of digital memory, preserved despite efforts to the contrary.

The officers approached. They claimed to detect the scent of marijuana drifting from the vehicle's interior — that familiar justification — and ordered its occupants to exit. Griffith refused, insisting she permitted no such substance in her car, demanding the production of an arrest warrant before she would comply. Wyne, aware of his status as a minor, agreed to emerge but imposed his own condition: no one would lay hands upon him until his mother arrived to witness whatever would unfold.

This resistance — modest, perhaps reasonable, certainly within the bounds of rights afforded even to the young — ignited an argument. Griffith's phone, propped upon the dashboard, recorded what came next. The officer's response was not negotiation but force: pepper spray discharged into the boy's face, chemical fire in his eyes. Then the Taser, its electrical charge convulsing through Wyne's body once, then twice. The footage captures his screams, his youth announced desperately: "I'm seventeen years old! Stop!"

Hands raised in surrender, the boy pleads — "Stop! Stop!" — but the officer's voice cuts through with a promise: "You're going to get it again." The threat becomes reality; the Taser fires once more.

The recording ceases when the officer discovers the phone, still witnessing from its perch. He seizes it, stops the documentation of his actions. Months would pass before Griffith discovered the footage lurking in her device's "Recently Deleted" folder — evidence nearly erased, almost lost.

Virginia Beach Police Chief Jim Cervera, reviewing what the lens preserved, offered careful words to the press: "There's some things I saw in that that I do not feel comfortable with." An investigation would examine not only the violence itself but whether tampering with evidence had occurred. The officer now occupies administrative duty, removed from the streets while questions multiply around what happened, what was recorded, and what someone tried to hide.
style_literary_T1.7.coling::5fe97409-ffd6-4931-b20b-8449a9ed:
Two bank robbers operating in Pennsylvania are believed to possess military or law enforcement training, and federal authorities have designated them armed and extremely dangerous. Throughout the early months of this year, a pair of masked men wielding handguns have struck three separate financial institutions in the Pittsburgh metropolitan area, their most recent incursion occurring on the tenth of April. These unknown assailants, captured on surveillance cameras as they press the muzzles of their weapons against the temples of terrified tellers, have not merely demanded cash—they have threatened to abduct employees from the premises and to open fire upon any officers who dare engage them in pursuit.

What distinguishes these criminals from common thugs, however, is the disciplined manner in which they manipulate their firearms, a detail that has prompted FBI investigators to theorize that the perpetrators may themselves be former law enforcement officials or veterans of military service. Scroll down for video footage of the incidents.

Authorities emphasize that these robberies, culminating most recently in the April tenth assault pictured in released surveillance images, have grown progressively more violent with each successive strike, the thieves now openly vocalizing their willingness to seize hostages and execute police personnel if confronted. Footage from bank security systems reveals one masked figure maintaining his trigger finger extended along the barrel of his pistol, just clear of the firing mechanism—a safety protocol drilled into those trained in official use of force. The men, garbed uniformly in dark sweatpants and sweatshirts, vault over counters with athletic efficiency as they initiate their raids.

"These individuals demonstrate firearms training of a specific character, suggesting backgrounds in military operations or law enforcement, whether former personnel or even current officers operating outside their authority," stated Patrick Fallon of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. "Street criminals rarely employ holsters," he remarked to WPXI reporters, noting another telling detail.

Both suspects stand approximately five feet eight inches to five feet nine inches in height and are described as maintaining excellent physical conditioning. During their methodical operations, one robber vaults behind the counter to gather currency while his accomplice menaces bank staff with his weapon trained upon them. The clothing worn during these crimes is believed to be swiftly discarded following each escape, and the perpetrators have selected an exceedingly common vehicle—a gray Toyota Corolla—for their flight from crime scenes.

Federal authorities have warned that these criminals grew increasingly aggressive and violent across their three documented strikes on January twenty-fourth, February twenty-first, and April tenth. The suspects are described as white males, five feet eight inches to five feet nine inches tall, of medium to larger build, and in excellent physical condition, according to CBS Pittsburgh. Both men are believed to be Pittsburgh natives, their regional accents evident on audio recordings. The FBI is offering ten thousand dollars for information leading to their capture.
style_literary_T1.7.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f:
Judith Scott, born May 1, 1943, and departed from this world March 15, 2005, emerged as an American fiber sculptor of international renown despite—or perhaps through—the twin conditions that marked her existence from birth: Down Syndrome and deafness. Her enrollment in 1987 at Oakland's Creative Growth Art Center, an institution dedicated to supporting individuals with developmental disabilities, marked the beginning of a profound transformation. There, within those walls devoted to artistic possibility, Judith discovered not merely a passion or talent for abstract fiber art, but an entirely new language through which she could communicate with a world that had long remained closed to her. Her twin sister Joyce would later chronicle this remarkable life in Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott, published in 2016, a testament to sibling devotion and artistic revelation.

Judith entered the world in Cincinnati, Ohio, on that spring day in 1943, arriving alongside her fraternal twin Joyce into a middle-class family that already included older brothers. Unlike Joyce, Judith bore from birth the chromosomal distinction of Down Syndrome. During infancy, she contracted Scarlet Fever, an illness that ravaged her hearing and left her deaf—though this devastating loss would remain unrecognized, misunderstood, undiagnosed for years to come. The first seven and a half years of Judith Scott's life unfolded within the domestic sphere, surrounded by parents, her twin sister, and brothers. Though the developmental differences between the two girls grew increasingly apparent with each passing month, their parents made conscious, deliberate efforts to treat these youngest family members with equality, refusing to let disability dictate affection or opportunity.

Yet when the time arrived for formal schooling, the limitations of mid-century educational systems revealed themselves with cruel efficiency. Judith was deemed "ineducable." The single classroom designated for children with disabilities required passage of verbally-based entrance examinations—tests that Judith, her deafness still unrecognized, could not possibly navigate successfully. Following medical counsel, her parents made the agonizing decision to place Judith in the Columbus State Institution, formerly known as the Columbus State School, a facility for the mentally disabled. The date was October 18, 1950, and this separation carved wounds into both twins that would persist for decades.

The institutional records from Judith Scott's early years at the Columbus facility paint a portrait shaped by profound misunderstanding. Based upon oral testing conducted before anyone recognized her deafness, she was assigned an IQ of 30—a number that became a cage, denying her any training opportunities, any chance for growth or development. Stripped of her twin, that other half of herself, Judith descended into severe alienation. Behavioral difficulties emerged and proliferated. Her Clinical Record, written in the flat, detached language of institutional bureaucracy, notes: "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Subsequently, administrators transferred her to a smaller state institution in Gallipolis, Ohio, as though distance might solve what isolation had created.

Thirty-five years passed. Thirty-five years of complete separation, of sisterhood severed. Then, in 1985, following lengthy and extraordinarily difficult negotiations with state bureaucracies, Joyce Scott succeeded in becoming her sister's legal guardian. She brought Judith to California, a state whose laws guaranteed all mentally disabled citizens access to ongoing education, to continued learning, to possibility. Judith Scott would die of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks shy of her sixty-second birthday, having outlived her birth life expectancy by nearly half a century.

On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott crossed the threshold of the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the world's pioneering organizations providing dedicated studio space for artists with disabilities. For almost two years, she displayed little interest in artistic activity of any kind. Paint left her unmoved. She scribbled loops and circles, but her work contained no representational imagery, nothing that suggested engagement or vision. Her disinterest grew so pronounced that staff members seriously considered terminating her involvement with the program entirely.

Then came the breakthrough, arriving as such moments often do—casually, unexpectedly, without fanfare. Judith observed a fiber art class conducted by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy. Something in those materials, in that process, ignited recognition within her. Using whatever lay at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of artistic expression. While other students stitched, she sculpted with unprecedented zeal and concentration, with an intensity that could not be ignored. Her creative gifts and absolute focus received immediate recognition, and she was granted complete freedom to select her own materials, to follow her vision wherever it led.

Taking whatever objects she found, regardless of ownership or conventional purpose, she would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns, creating diverse sculptures of many different shapes and sizes. Some resemble cocoons or body parts, organic forms that speak to transformation and embodiment. Others rise as elongated totemic poles, vertical assertions of presence. Many works feature pairs—twin forms reflecting Scott's experience as a twin, that fundamental relationship severed for three and a half decades. Judith worked on her art five days weekly for eighteen years, an extraordinary sustained period of productivity that yielded over two hundred pieces in total.

Her first exhibition arrived in 1999, coinciding with publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events propelled her toward worldwide recognition, toward visibility long denied. Scott's work achieved immense popularity within the world of outsider art, and her pieces command substantial sums at auction and in galleries. She is now celebrated as a contemporary artist, no longer confined to the category of outsider, her work held in permanent collections at prestigious institutions: the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan, the American Visionary Art Museum in Baltimore, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art in Manhattan, Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art in Chicago, Irish Museum of Modern Art in Dublin, The Oakland Museum, L'Aracine Musée D'Art Brut in Paris, Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection in Paris and Prague, and Collection de l'art brut in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Her exhibition history includes notable presentations: Judith Scott: Touchdown at Creative Growth Art Center in 2018, Bound and Unbound at Brooklyn Museum in 2014-15, retrospectives at Ricco Maresca Gallery in 2009 and 2002, and participation in the 57th Venice Biennale in 2017, among many others spanning continents and decades, testimony to an artist who found her voice through fiber, transformation, and wrapping the world in her vision.
